es.summary: El hipotiroidismo es la deficiencia de hormonas tiroideas (T3, T4) que reduce el metabolismo corporal. Se manifiesta con fatiga, aumento de peso y intolerancia al frío.
key_points: TSH elevado y T4 libre bajo son hallazgos de laboratorio típicos.
La enfermedad de Hashimoto es la causa autoinmune más frecuente.
El tratamiento de primera línea es levotiroxina oral.
Complicación grave: coma mixedémico, que requiere atención de urgencia.
El control regular de TSH es esencial para ajustar la dosis.

pathophysiology: Disminuye la síntesis de T3 y T4.
El hipotálamo aumenta la liberación de TRH.
La hipófisis eleva la secreción de TSH en respuesta.
Metabolismo basal se reduce, afectando todos los órganos.
risk_factors: Exposición a radiación cervical o tratamientos con yodo.
Enfermedades autoinmunes (p. ej., lupus, artritis reumatoide).
Uso crónico de litio, amiodarona o interferón.
signs_symptoms: Aumento de peso y edema facial leve.
Intolerancia al frío y piel seca.
Estreñimiento, caída del cabello y menorragia.
diagnostics: Perfil lipídico con colesterol LDL elevado.
treatment: Reevaluar TSH cada 6‑8 semanas hasta estabilizar.
Corregir deficiencias de yodo solo si están presentes.
Educación sobre toma correcta del fármaco.
nursing_care: Evaluar signos vitales, especialmente temperatura y frecuencia cardíaca.
Observar cambios en la piel, cabello y patrón intestinal.
Revisar resultados de TSH y T4 libre según orden médica.
Administrar levotiroxina 30 min antes del desayuno.
patient_teaching: Tomar levotiroxina con el estómago vacío, 30 min antes de alimentos.
Evitar calcio, hierro o suplementos de soja dentro de 4 h de la dosis.
Informar signos de sobredosis (palpitaciones, temblores) o insuficiencia (fatiga extrema).
Acudir a controles de laboratorio cada 6‑8 semanas.
Mantener una dieta balanceada y ejercicio moderado.

evidenced_by: cansancio al realizar actividades de la vida diaria
disminución de la tolerancia al ejercicio
outcomes: Actividad tolerada sin fatiga excesiva: paciente completa ADL con mínima fatiga en 2 semanas
Frecuencia cardíaca en reposo entre 60‑80 lat/min al final de la semana 3

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de energía antes y después de actividades diarias
interventions.rationale: Permite identificar límites funcionales y planificar descansos

interventions.action: Programar períodos de descanso cada 30‑45 min durante actividades prolongadas
interventions.rationale: Previene agotamiento y mejora la tolerancia al esfuerzo

interventions.action: Enseñar técnicas de conservación de energía (sentarse al cocinar, usar ayudas de movilidad)
interventions.rationale: Reduce la demanda física y conserva energía

interventions.action: Monitorear signos vitales (FC, presión arterial) antes y después del ejercicio
interventions.rationale: Detecta bradicardia o descompensación cardiovascular

interventions.action: Coordinar con el médico para ajustar la dosis de levotiroxina si persiste intolerancia
interventions.rationale: Optimiza el control hormonal y mejora la capacidad funcional

outcomes: Electrolitos séricos dentro de rangos normales (Na 135‑145 mEq/L) en 4 semanas
Sin signos clínicos de hiponatremia ni hipoglucemia durante la hospitalización

interventions.action: Obtener y registrar niveles de Na, K, glucosa cada 48 h
interventions.rationale: Detecta alteraciones tempranas y permite intervención oportuna

interventions.action: Evaluar ingesta y pérdida de líquidos, registrar balance hídrico
interventions.rationale: Ayuda a prevenir retención excesiva o deshidratación

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre evitar consumo excesivo de agua sin reposición de electrolitos
interventions.rationale: Reduce riesgo de hiponatremia dilucional

interventions.action: Revisar interacciones de levotiroxina con suplementos de calcio o hierro
interventions.rationale: Previene alteraciones en absorción y posibles desequilibrios

interventions.action: Notificar al médico cualquier valor de Na < 130 mEq/L o glucosa < 70 mg/dL
interventions.rationale: Facilita intervención médica inmediata

en.summary: Hypothyroidism is the deficiency of thyroid hormones (T3, T4) that reduces body metabolism. It presents with fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance.
key_points: Elevated TSH and low free T4 are typical laboratory findings.
Hashimoto disease is the most common autoimmune cause.
Severe complication: myxedema coma, requiring emergency care.
Regular TSH monitoring is essential to adjust the dose.

pathophysiology: Decreases synthesis of T3 and T4.
The pituitary raises TSH secretion in response.
Basal metabolism is reduced, affecting all organs.
risk_factors: Exposure to cervical radiation or iodine treatments.
Other autoimmune diseases (e.g., lupus, rheumatoid arthritis).
Chronic use of lithium, amiodarone, or interferon.
signs_symptoms: Weight gain and mild facial edema.
diagnostics: Lipid profile with elevated LDL cholesterol.
treatment: Reevaluate TSH every 6‑8 weeks until stable.
Correct iodine deficiency only if present.
nursing_care: Assess vital signs, especially temperature and heart rate.
Observe changes in skin, hair, and bowel pattern.
Review TSH and free T4 results as ordered.
patient_teaching: Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, 30 min before meals.
Avoid calcium, iron, or soy supplements within 4 h of dose.
Report overdose signs (palpitations, tremors) or deficiency (excessive fatigue).
Maintain a balanced diet and moderate exercise.

outcomes: Activity tolerated without excessive fatigue: patient completes ADL with minimal fatigue in 2 weeks
Resting heart rate 60‑80 beats/min by week 3

interventions.action: Assess energy level before and after daily activities
interventions.rationale: Identifies functional limits and plans rest periods

interventions.action: Schedule rest periods every 30‑45 min during prolonged activities
interventions.rationale: Prevents exhaustion and improves exercise tolerance

interventions.action: Teach energy conservation techniques (sitting while cooking, using mobility aids)
interventions.rationale: Reduces physical demand and conserves energy

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs (HR, BP) before and after exercise
interventions.rationale: Detects bradycardia or cardiovascular decompensation

interventions.action: Coordinate with physician to adjust levothyroxine dose if intolerance persists
interventions.rationale: Optimizes hormonal control and improves functional capacity

outcomes: Serum electrolytes within normal ranges (Na 135‑145 mEq/L) in 4 weeks
No clinical signs of hyponatremia or hypoglycemia during hospitalization

interventions.action: Obtain and record Na, K, glucose levels every 48 h
interventions.rationale: Detects early changes and allows timely intervention

interventions.action: Assess fluid intake and output, record fluid balance
interventions.rationale: Helps prevent excessive retention or dehydration

interventions.action: Educate patient on avoiding excessive water intake without electrolyte replacement
interventions.rationale: Reduces risk of dilutional hyponatremia

interventions.action: Review levothyroxine interactions with calcium or iron supplements
interventions.rationale: Prevents absorption alterations and potential imbalances

interventions.action: Notify physician of any Na < 130 mEq/L or glucose < 70 mg/dL
interventions.rationale: Facilitates immediate medical intervention

key_points.1.quote: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism.

key_points.4.quote: About 6 to 8 weeks after you start taking the medicine, you will get a blood test to check your thyroid hormone level.

sections.pathophysiology.2.quote: The hypothalamus releases thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) which stimulates the pituitary gland to release TSH, which stimulates the thyroid to release T3 and T4.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: In response to TRH, the anterior pituitary gland releases thyrotropin, also known as thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: You are at higher risk for hypothyroidism if you: Are a woman Are older than age 60 Have had a thyroid problem before, such as a goiter Have had surgery to correct a thyroid problem Have received radiation treatment to the thyroid, neck, or chest Have a family history of thyroid disease Were pregnant or had a baby in the past 6 months Have Turner syndrome , a genetic disorder that affects females Have pernicious anemia , in which the body cannot

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: Hyperthyroidism Hypothyroidism Nervousness/irritability Fatigue/muscle weakness Mood swings Heat intolerance Insomnia Tremors Tachycardia/irregular heart rhythm Weight loss Diarrhea Goiter Depression Fatigue Dry skin Dry, thinning hair Cold intolerance Puffy face Joint/muscle pain Bradycardia Decreased sweating Constipation Heavy/irregular menstrual periods and fertility problems Table 21.9 Signs and Symptoms of Hyperthyroidism and Hypothyroidism

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: The symptoms of hypothyroidism can vary from person to person and may include: Fatigue Weight gain A puffy face Trouble tolerating cold Joint and muscle pain Constipation Dry skin Dry, thinning hair Decreased sweating Heavy or irregular menstrual periods Fertility problems in women Depression Slowed heart rate Goiter, an enlarged thyroid that may cause your neck to look swollen.

sections.treatment.0.quote: Hypothyroidism is primarily treated with thyroid hormone replacement therapy, such as levothyroxine.

sections.treatment.1.quote: Initial bloodwork to monitor thyroid hormone levels and taper levothyroxine dosing are completed every four to eight weeks until a target level is reached, then bloodwork is checked at six months, then yearly.

sections.complications.0.quote: If hypothyroidism is left untreated, the client may develop a myxedema coma , which is a life-threatening disorder that leads to hypothermia, cardiovascular collapse, hypoventilation, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and coma.

sections.nursing_care.2.quote: The symptoms of hypothyroidism can vary from person to person and may include: Fatigue Weight gain A puffy face Trouble tolerating cold Joint and muscle pain Constipation Dry skin Dry, thinning hair Decreased sweating Heavy or irregular menstrual periods Fertility problems in women Depression Slowed heart rate Goiter, an enlarged thyroid that may cause your neck to look swollen.

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: The patient should be able to state the importance of therapy compliance, maintain a positive body image, and state what symptoms should be reported to the provider, such as changes in weight, energy levels, and mood, with specific attention to symptoms like rapid heartbeat or tremors in hyperthyroidism, and fatigue or weight gain in hypothyroidism.

sections.patient_teaching.3.quote: Initial bloodwork to monitor thyroid hormone levels and taper levothyroxine dosing are completed every four to eight weeks until a target level is reached, then bloodwork is checked at six months, then yearly.
